@dfelinto @andrewpprice @GregFeingold No MCP and no Blender UI at all. I ran Fable 5.1 in a sandboxed Linux box with a shell. It installed Blender, wrote a Python script against Blender's built-in bpy API. And rendered everything CPU only. No asset library used either.

Super bullish on WebMCP. Much like Tesla FSD meets the world where it is (streets, stoplights, potholes and all), agents *need* to ride the existing WWW infrastructure… WebMCP makes it more efficient.

Some pretty unique wins too. e.g: Next.js dev pages could expose debugging tools directly to agents in the specific tab they’re testing, with page-specific context, instead of sifting through server logs. No separate MCP server to find and configure because the page directly exposes its own 'agent tools'.

e.g: in this world 𝚏𝚡 + 𝚊𝚐𝚎𝚗𝚝-𝚋𝚛𝚘𝚠𝚜𝚎𝚛 is a complete web dev stack with zero loss in debugging depth

The unexpected benefit of open source is that it allows model training companies to train on using your software (and optimizing it) for free.

Blender may have just won as a 3D asset creation software because the models will be better at using it than any proprietary ones

Marvin Minsky wrote about this in The Emotion Machine. Emotions are a core part of human intelligence, not some epiphenomenal side effect of human evolution (which presumably many AI folks believe it is).

Minsky describes a selector of sorts for different thinking strategies.

Ken Thompson’s “Reflections on Trusting Trust” feels super relevant to AI.

He bootstrapped a “poisoned” compiler that left no traces of the poison in the source code because it compiled itself.

You can imagine the same thing happening with models where one poisoned generation helps train the next while removing any traces of the poison.
